9729.title: INVEST Criteria
9729.heading: INVEST Criteria
9729.content:
INVEST is a quality check for user stories: Independent, Negotiable, Valuable, Estimable, Sized appropriately, and Testable. The criteria reveal stories that are overly coupled, prescriptive, unclear in value, too uncertain, too large, or impossible to verify.

They are diagnostic rather than rigid rules. A story can temporarily violate a criterion while the team uses refinement, a [[Spike]], or conversation to improve it.

9735.content: An inverse-square law has the form $y=k/x^2$. Doubling the distance variable reduces the dependent quantity to one quarter. Plotting $y$ against $1/x^2$ produces a straight line through the origin when the relationship holds. Such laws commonly arise when a conserved influence spreads across spherical area proportional to $x^2$.

9738.title: Inverse Programming
9738.heading: Inverse Programming
9738.content:
Inverse programming composes a model by using the result of one probabilistic question as a factor within another description. It lets an inference developed for one direction or subsystem become reusable knowledge in a larger model.

The called program remains a probabilistic relation rather than a deterministic return value. When the outer inference evaluates that factor, it may trigger the inner question for the conditioning values currently under consideration.

9741.sourceSearchName: inverse power method inverse power method
9741.title: Inverse Power Method
9741.heading: Inverse Power Method
9741.content:
The inverse power method applies the [[Power Method]] to $A^{-1}$ without explicitly forming the inverse. Each iteration solves a system with coefficient matrix $A$.

Because the eigenvalues of $A^{-1}$ are reciprocals of those of $A$, the method converges toward the eigenvector associated with the smallest-magnitude eigenvalue of $A$, under the required dominance conditions.

9744.title: Inverse Function
9744.heading: Inverse Function
9744.content: An inverse function reverses a one-to-one function: $f^{-1}(f(x))=x$ on the original domain. Its graph is the reflection of the original graph across $y=x$, and its domain and range are exchanged. A function must assign distinct outputs to distinct inputs, or its domain must be restricted before an inverse can be defined.

9747.title: Inverse Element
9747.heading: Inverse Element
9747.content:
The inverse of a group element a is the unique element a⁻¹ satisfying aa⁻¹ = a⁻¹a = e. Under additive notation it is written -a.

The inverse of a product reverses order: (ab)⁻¹ = b⁻¹a⁻¹.

9750.title: Inverse Distance Weighting
9750.heading: Inverse Distance Weighting
9750.content: Inverse distance weighting estimates an unsampled location as a weighted average of nearby observations, giving closer points more influence than distant ones. The distance exponent controls how quickly influence declines. The method produces a [[Point-Surface Interpolation|surface]] without explicitly modeling spatial covariance, so it can create local bull's-eye patterns and provides no automatic account of prediction uncertainty. Its output should be interpreted in light of sampling density.

9756.title: Intrusion Detection System
9756.heading: Intrusion Detection System
9756.content:
An intrusion detection system analyzes activity to identify possible attacks, misuse, or behavior inconsistent with authorized use. It can examine firewall, server, identity, and service logs for repeated login failures, unusual traffic, or attempts to retrieve inappropriate data.

Detection turns raw operational records into security alerts that people or automated systems can investigate. It reports suspicious behavior; an [[Intrusion Prevention System]] additionally acts to block or contain it.

At the network layer, an intrusion detection system searches traffic for suspicious activity and known threats and records an alert when it finds them. Its evidence can feed [[Security Event Monitoring]] so observations from the network can be correlated with host and application activity.

9759.title: Intrusion Prevention System
9759.heading: Intrusion Prevention System
9759.content:
An intrusion prevention system detects suspicious activity and automatically intervenes to stop or limit it. An action can deny further logins, block traffic, isolate a source, or otherwise prevent the suspected use from continuing.

Automated prevention must use rules calibrated to the service because false positives can deny legitimate access. Monitoring and retained evidence are still required so administrators can understand why the action occurred and improve the control.

The source describes an intrusion prevention system as combining detection with firewall-like intervention. When its detector identifies a matching intrusion, the preventive component can stop the activity automatically instead of waiting for a person to respond to an alert.

9762.title: Intrinsic Skill Required
9762.heading: Intrinsic Skill Required
9762.content:
Intrinsic skill required is the amount of ability needed to overcome a challenge when time pressure is removed. It isolates the precision, reasoning, memory, or coordination demand from the stress of having to act quickly.

Separating skill from time pressure helps tune difficulty. A task can require sophisticated execution but little stress, or simple execution under severe stress.

9765.title: Intrinsic Semiconductor
9765.heading: Intrinsic Semiconductor
9765.content: An intrinsic semiconductor is a semiconductor in its pure form, before controlled impurities are added. Its [[Semiconductor Band Gap]] keeps most electrons out of the conduction band at low temperature. Thermal energy can promote some electrons across the gap, creating mobile electrons and corresponding holes. Deliberate [[Semiconductor Doping]] changes this behavior far more strongly for device construction.

9768.title: Intrinsic Motivation
9768.heading: Intrinsic Motivation
9768.content:
Intrinsic motivation comes from the value and satisfaction of the activity itself. In creative work it is supported by autonomy over meaningful choices, growing mastery of a craft, and a clear purpose connecting effort to a larger result.

External rewards and controls can support necessary boundaries, but excessive task assignment and surveillance weaken ownership. Self-managing teams give motivation a structure in which it can become coordinated value.

9771.sourceSearchName: intransitive game balance intransitive game balance
9771.title: Intransitive Game Balance
9771.heading: Intransitive Game Balance
9771.content:
In the source's terminology, intransitive game balance allows some parts to be plainly more capable than others. Overall balance is achieved by making greater benefits carry proportionately greater costs.

This structure appears in progression systems, where later objects or abilities are intended to be more powerful. A [[Progression Curve]] coordinates cost and benefit so every part retains a viable role at the appropriate point in play.

9774.title: Intractable Problem
9774.heading: Intractable Problem
9774.content:
An intractable problem is one for which the best known exact algorithms require an impractical amount of time on nontrivial inputs. The problem may be clearly defined and solvable in principle while still resisting useful computation at scale.

Intractability shifts attention from merely finding any [[Algorithm]] to finding a different kind of result. An [[Approximation Algorithm]] may return a solution close enough to the optimum, or analysis may establish useful bounds on how far that result can be from the best possible one.

9777.heading: Intrinsic Limit of Law
9777.content:
An intrinsic limit of law is a boundary that follows from the conditions under which a legal order can govern persons, rather than from a discretionary policy choice. The source argues that privacy can function as such a limit in an age of extensive data collection.

If law reaches every aspect of thought and conduct, the autonomy required to form intentions and direct a life is weakened. The limit protects a domain in which people can exist as agents subject to law rather than merely as objects of observation.

9783.title: Intonation
9783.heading: Intonation
9783.content:
Intonation is the pattern of pitch movement across an utterance. Along with loudness and duration, it signals phrasing, emphasis, sentence type, attitude, and conversational intent.

A [[Text-to-Speech]] system must predict intonation from text and context rather than pronounce every word with a flat contour. Poor prosody can make otherwise correct synthetic speech difficult or unpleasant to interpret.

9786.title: Interpreted Story
9786.heading: Interpreted Story
9786.content:
An interpreted story arises from the combination of authored material, systemic events, and the player's understanding. Its building blocks may be shared by every player, while their arrangement and meaning vary with choices, attention, and imagination.

This form sits between a fixed [[Authored Story]] and a highly [[Open Story]]. The creator supplies characters, rules, and signals, but the player connects them into a particular account of what happened and why it mattered.

9789.title: Interval Notation
9789.heading: Interval Notation
9789.content: Interval notation describes a connected portion of the [[Real Number Line]]. Square brackets include a finite endpoint, parentheses exclude it, and infinity always receives a parenthesis because it is not a real endpoint. Intersections retain only values shared by every interval, while unions collect values belonging to at least one interval.

9792.title: Interval
9792.heading: Interval
9792.content:
An interval is a set of real numbers containing every real number between any two of its members. It represents a continuous portion of the [[Number Line]] and therefore contains infinitely many values even when its length is finite.

Intervals may be [[Bounded Interval]]s with two finite boundaries or [[Unbounded Interval]]s extending indefinitely. Each finite boundary can be included or excluded, represented by a [[Closed Endpoint]] or [[Open Endpoint]]. Linear inequality solution sets commonly form intervals or unions of intervals.

9795.sourceSearchName: intersection of sets intersection of sets
9795.title: Intersection of Sets
9795.heading: Intersection of Sets
9795.content:
The intersection of sets contains exactly the elements common to all of them. Intersections preserve many closure properties, so intersecting subgroups, subrings, or subfields again produces the corresponding substructure.

This makes intersection a natural way to define the smallest structure satisfying stated containment requirements.

For two sets, A ∩ B = {x | x ∈ A ∧ x ∈ B}; its definition mirrors logical conjunction. Sets are disjoint exactly when their intersection is empty.

9798.title: Interpolation
9798.heading: Interpolation
9798.content:
Interpolation estimates a function value at a point inside the range of known data. It constructs a function that agrees with the supplied data values and evaluates that function between them.

[[Polynomial Interpolation]] is convenient because polynomials are easy to evaluate, differentiate, and integrate. The distinction from extrapolation is that interpolation stays within the span of the known independent-variable values.

9801.title: Interpolation Artifact
9801.heading: Interpolation Artifact
9801.content:
An interpolation artifact is a dependency among neighboring pixel values created when a resampling method estimates samples at noninteger positions. Nearest-neighbor, bilinear, and bicubic interpolation use different neighborhoods and therefore leave different combinations of blockiness, smoothing, and correlation.

The artifact can be subtle or invisible to direct inspection while remaining statistically detectable. Sharpening, noise, compression, and repeated transformations can weaken or obscure it, so the absence of a detected artifact does not rule out resampling.

9804.title: Interpolating Polynomial
9804.heading: Interpolating Polynomial
9804.content:
An interpolating polynomial $p_n$ satisfies $p_n(x_i)=f(x_i)$ at each of $n+1$ distinct data points. Its degree is at most $n$.

The polynomial is unique: if two degree-$n$ polynomials agree at $n+1$ distinct points, their difference has too many roots unless it is identically zero. Different interpolation formulas reorganize the same result.

9807.heading: Interocular Distance and Depth Scale
9807.content: The horizontal distance between the cameras of a stereo pair is its interocular distance. Increasing or decreasing that separation changes the amount of parallax and thus the apparent depth scale, even when the 3D geometry stays the same. The book notes that nearby subjects show stronger differences than remote ones at a human-like separation and that deliberately unnatural camera spacing can exaggerate depth or create a miniaturized impression. Camera spacing should be chosen with the shot's composition and [[Stereo Window Placement]] in mind.

Interpersonal influence measures how another user's relationship and prior interactions affect a receiver's decision. A sender who is a close friend, authority, or consistently successful recommender may receive more weight.

Influence differs from [[Individual Preference]] because it concerns who supplied the item rather than what the item contains. Social models can learn both factors and combine them when estimating adoption.

9813.heading: Internet Robustness and Military Origins
9813.content:
Early packet-network research emphasized communications that could continue despite failed links or disrupted infrastructure. Distributed routing and independently forwarded packets avoided dependence on one permanent circuit.

Military crisis concerns influenced this objective, but the modern Internet is far more than a defense system. Commercial, academic, technical, and social institutions reshaped the network after its original design.

9816.title: Internet Protocol
9816.heading: Internet Protocol
9816.content:
Internet Protocol addresses and routes packets from a source host toward a destination across interconnected networks. Each packet carries enough header information for routers to forward it independently.

IP provides best-effort delivery rather than guaranteeing arrival or order. Higher-level protocols such as [[Transmission Control Protocol]] add reliability when an application requires it.

For a networked game, IP supplies the addressed packet layer beneath transports such as TCP and [[User Datagram Protocol]]. IPv4 and IPv6 use different address sizes, so application code should avoid assuming one fixed endpoint representation.

9819.content:
Internet of Things security addresses networks of connected sensors, appliances, controllers, and other specialized devices. Their scale, varied ownership, physical exposure, and uneven maintenance make familiar weaknesses difficult to manage consistently.

An insecure device can endanger its owner and become infrastructure for attacks elsewhere. The [[Mirai Botnet]] demonstrates why unique credentials, safe defaults, updates, segmentation, and monitoring must be designed across the device ecosystem.

Internet of Things legal risk arises when connected physical devices continuously collect information, exchange it, and use it to affect their surroundings. The same device can implicate privacy, safety, evidence, security, and product responsibility.

Because collection may be ambient and action may be automated, users may not see when a legally significant operation occurs. The activity-based view separates sensing, processing, storage, distribution, and physical action so responsibility can be traced.

The Internet of Services is the collection of networked services that monitor, support, bill for, or otherwise act on behalf of connected devices. A printer service can track supplies and usage; a streetlight service can detect failed lamps and organize maintenance.

The device supplies observations or accepts control, while the service performs the surrounding business process. This complements a network of connected things by giving their data an operational purpose.

9831.content:
Internet governance shifted from United States defense management to the National Science Foundation and later toward commerce agencies and specialized coordinating institutions. Responsibilities included addressing, names, standards, and backbone policy.

The transition reflects that the Internet is a political and institutional system as well as a technical one. Control of shared identifiers and interconnection rules affects who can participate.

9834.heading: Internet Control Message Protocol
9834.content:
Internet Control Message Protocol carries diagnostic and error information associated with Internet Protocol delivery. Echo request and reply messages support tools that test reachability and estimate round-trip time.

ICMP is not the transport for gameplay state, but its responses can help diagnose connectivity. Firewalls may block or limit messages, so lack of an echo reply does not prove that a game service is unavailable.

9837.heading: Internet Backbone Topology
9837.content:
Internet backbones are high-capacity long-distance networks that carry traffic among regional and local networks. The topology evolved from a small mesh of research machines into hierarchical connections spanning the globe.

Fiber-optic links and large server centers replaced slow leased lines and isolated mainframes. End devices reach a local network, then a regional provider, and eventually one or more backbones.

9846.title: Internal Playtest
9846.heading: Internal Playtest
9846.content:
An internal playtest is performed by the designers or development team. It supports fast iteration on an unfinished artifact and checks whether a build is coherent enough to expose to people outside the project.

Familiarity makes internal testers efficient but biased. They know the intended controls and goals, so an internal success cannot establish that a new player will understand the same experience.

9849.title: Internal Economy
9849.heading: Internal Economy
9849.content:
An internal economy is the part of a game's core mechanics that governs numeric relationships among entities and how those relationships change over time. It tracks resources as they are produced, consumed, converted, moved, or exchanged.

The economy is broader than money. Health, ammunition, time, labor, territory, and other quantified entities can participate when mechanics change their amounts.

9858.content: If a real-valued function is continuous on $[a,b]$, then it takes every value between $f(a)$ and $f(b)$. Thus, for any intermediate value $v$, some $c$ in $(a,b)$ satisfies $f(c)=v$. A sign change across the endpoints therefore guarantees at least one zero inside the interval.

9861.title: Intermediate Language
9861.heading: Intermediate Language
9861.content:
A .NET language compiler translates source code into intermediate language instructions stored in an assembly. The runtime loads that assembly and compiles the IL into native instructions for the current processor before execution.

This intermediate representation separates the source language from the machine architecture. Different .NET languages can target the same runtime services, and one compiled assembly can remain portable where a compatible runtime supplies the required APIs.

9864.title: Interlayer Edge
9864.heading: Interlayer Edge
9864.content:
An interlayer edge connects nodes belonging to different network layers. It may identify the same entity across contexts, represent a dependency, or express an interaction between different systems.

Interlayer meaning cannot be inferred from its existence alone. Dependency edges propagate failure differently from ordinary interaction edges, while identity edges couple copies of one node through time or relationship layers.

9867.title: Interface Segregation Principle
9867.heading: Interface Segregation Principle
9867.content: The interface segregation principle keeps a contract focused on operations its consumers actually need. A read-only inventory command should depend on a read interface, while a command that changes quantity depends on a write interface; neither needs to see an unrelated method. Smaller role-specific interfaces reduce coupling and make tests and future refactoring more precise.

9870.title: Interjection Handler
9870.heading: Interjection Handler
9870.content:
An interjection handler is reusable dialog logic that detects and responds to interruptions such as help, repeat, correction, or cancellation. It can be available from many states without duplicating the same transitions everywhere.

The handler must preserve enough [[Conversation Context]] to resume safely when appropriate. Some interjections instead require clearing state or transferring control to a different [[Assistant Skill]].

9873.title: Interjection
9873.heading: Interjection
9873.content:
An interjection is a user contribution that interrupts or temporarily departs from the current dialog flow. It can request help, repeat information, correct a value, cancel, or start a new goal.

Handling interjections makes a conversation less rigid than a single-path form. After the interruption, the [[Dialog Manager]] must decide whether to resume, revise, or abandon the prior task.

9876.content:
An interest point detector locates image positions with distinctive local structure that can be found again under changed viewing conditions. Corners and blob-like regions are useful because their location is better constrained than a uniform patch or straight edge alone.

AR tracking needs detectors that balance repeatability, localization accuracy, computation, and invariance to scale or viewpoint. Each detected point becomes the center of a feature descriptor used for matching.

9879.sourceSearchName: interdisciplinary ai ethics interdisciplinary ai ethics
9879.title: Interdisciplinary AI Ethics
9879.heading: Interdisciplinary AI Ethics
9879.content:
Interdisciplinary AI ethics combines technical, legal, philosophical, social-scientific, and practical knowledge to evaluate intelligent systems. No single field can understand both how a model works and how it changes institutions, rights, behavior, and power.

Transdisciplinary work extends the collaboration beyond academic fields to professionals, users, and affected communities. The challenge is not merely placing experts in the same room; they need shared methods and enough mutual understanding to connect abstract principles with concrete development. [[AI Ethics Education]] builds this capacity, while stakeholder participation prevents expert collaboration from excluding lived consequences.

9882.title: Interdependent Network
9882.heading: Interdependent Network
9882.content:
An interdependent network contains nodes in one layer whose operation depends on nodes in another. A communication router may depend on a power station, while the power system may depend on communication control.

Dependency edges allow failure to propagate back and forth between layers. This coupling can make the combined system more fragile than either network analyzed separately.

9885.title: Interactivity
9885.heading: Interactivity
9885.content:
Interactivity is a reciprocal cycle in which two or more agents act on and affect one another in a contextually related way. In a game, player input changes the game state and the game's feedback changes the player's mental state.

This reciprocity distinguishes interaction from one-way reaction. The resulting [[Game-Player System]] can carry several nested timescales, from rapid [[Action-Feedback Interactivity]] to slower cognitive, social, emotional, and cultural loops.

9888.title: Interconnected Network
9888.heading: Interconnected Network
9888.content:
An interconnected network is a family of layer graphs whose nodes interact across layers. Cross-layer edges represent those interactions but do not necessarily mean that one endpoint functionally depends on the other.

This distinction separates ordinary coupling from an [[Interdependent Network]]. Node or layer labels can identify which subsystem each endpoint belongs to.

9891.title: Interactivity Budget
9891.heading: Interactivity Budget
9891.content:
An interactivity budget is the finite amount of perceptual, cognitive, social, and emotional effort a player is willing and able to devote at a moment. Fast reflexive interactions often consume capacity before slower reflective ones can operate.

Designers allocate this budget by deciding which loops are intense at the same time and by separating competing demands across time. Exceeding it creates confusion or exhaustion; using too little can produce boredom and weak [[Engagement]].

9893.sourceSearchName: interactive voice response system interactive voice response system
9893.title: Interactive Voice Response System
9893.heading: Document

9894.sourceSearchName: interactive voice response system interactive voice response system
9894.title: Interactive Voice Response System
9894.heading: Interactive Voice Response System
9894.content:
An interactive voice response system conducts automated telephone interactions through spoken prompts and user responses. Traditional systems often accept keypad input or restricted speech and use a controlled call-flow to route or complete a service task.

An IVR is a form of [[Virtual Agent]]. Its constrained [[Directed Dialog]] makes recognition and recovery more manageable than the broad, open requests expected by a [[Personal Virtual Assistant]].

Common operations include [[Temporal Hover Readout|hover readout]], [[Temporal Zooming|zooming]], series highlighting, and range selection. Interaction can expose detail without placing every label on the static figure, but the initial view still needs a clear scale and overview. Essential meaning should not depend on an undiscoverable control.

Selecting an entry can apply [[Time-Series Highlighting]], hide a series, or restore it to a crowded display. This reduces overplotting while keeping all series available. The current visibility state must remain apparent, and interaction should supplement rather than replace meaningful labels because a long legend can itself become difficult to scan.

9903.content: An interactive space-time cube represents two spatial dimensions and time as three orthogonal axes without first aggregating a dimension. The cube can be rotated, moved, and zoomed, while keyboard controls select visible slices along each axis. Different orientations resemble alternative [[Hovmoller Diagram|Hovmoller views]]. The cube preserves the full array conceptually but suffers from occlusion and perspective, so two-dimensional reductions remain important.

Dragging its boundaries can couple range selection with [[Temporal Zooming]], filtering, or a summary calculation. 9909.title: Interactive Story
9909.heading: Interactive Story
9909.content:
An interactive story combines a credible sequence of dramatically meaningful events with player participation. Player events contribute to the experience, and [[Dramatic Action|dramatic actions]] may alter the future plot.

Interactivity does not require every action to change the story. The design decides which choices are dramatically significant while preserving gameplay as the reason the audience is playing rather than watching.

9912.title: Interactive Computing
9912.heading: Interactive Computing
9912.content:
Interactive computing lets a user issue an action and receive a response quickly enough to guide the next action. It replaces the delayed submit-and-wait cycle of batch processing with an ongoing conversation.

Terminals, displays, time-sharing, minicomputers, and personal machines each advanced this mode. Interactivity changed software from a finished calculation into an environment for exploration.

9915.content: A muzzle-flash footage element needs an appropriate scale, timing, color, and position at the barrel, but a bright flash should also briefly change nearby illumination. The book duplicates foreground and background plates, uses soft roto mattes to isolate wall and actor regions facing the flash, and raises their exposure only for the flash frames. A cast shadow can complete the exchange between the light source and the scene. The brief change must occur in the right locations rather than brighten every pixel equally.

9918.title: Interactive Map
9918.heading: Interactive Map
9918.content: An interactive map supports operations such as panning, zooming, selecting features, and requesting details. It can combine tiled [[Reference Map|reference maps]] with thematic points, polygons, or rasters. Interaction makes dense attributes available through [[Spatial Tooltip|tooltips]] and [[Map Popup Graphic|popups]], but the initial extent, legend, and visible layers must still communicate the map's purpose. Controls should preserve awareness of scale and location as the view changes.

9921.title: Interactive Hierarchical Clustering
9921.heading: Interactive Hierarchical Clustering
9921.content:
Interactive hierarchical clustering allows users to inspect and revise merges, splits, or branch priorities while a cluster tree is constructed or explored. Domain knowledge can prevent an implausible early merge from constraining every higher level.

User edits may be encoded as constraints and propagated to later decisions. The system should show the structural consequences of an intervention because changing one branch can alter feasible groupings elsewhere in the hierarchy.

9924.heading: Inter-Attribute Summary
9924.content:
An inter-attribute summary stores strongly connected value pairs drawn from two different categorical attributes together with their supported co-occurrence counts. Weak pairs below the threshold are omitted.

CACTUS can construct these sparse summaries in a scan of the data and use them during later projection and clustering phases.

9927.title: Interaction Technique
9927.heading: Interaction Technique
9927.content:
An interaction technique is a method that lets a user accomplish a task through a [[User Interface]]. It includes hardware and software: an [[Input Device]] captures user information, software maps that information to an action, and an [[Output Device]] presents the system's response.

The same device can support many techniques, and the same technique can sometimes be implemented with different devices. What matters is whether the mapping is natural, efficient, and appropriate for the task. In a [[3D User Interface]], major technique families support [[3D Manipulation]], [[3D Travel]], [[Wayfinding]], and [[System Control]].

9929.sourceSearchName: interaction layer of play interaction layer of play
9929.title: Interaction Layer of Play
9929.heading: Document

9930.sourceSearchName: interaction layer of play interaction layer of play
9930.title: Interaction Layer of Play
9930.heading: Interaction Layer of Play
9930.content:
The interaction layer is the player's understanding of what can be done and how an action changes the game. It joins perceived [[Affordance|affordances]], controls, rules, and [[Feedback]] into a usable relationship between intention and result.

Good interaction reduces avoidable effort between deciding and acting. Consistency lets previous learning carry forward, while navigability helps the player locate a coherent path through the possibility space.

9931.title: Interaction Layer of Play

9933.title: Intent
9933.heading: Intent
9933.content:
An intent is the action or goal an assistant assigns to a user's utterance. Examples include requesting weather, sending a message, or reserving a table, independent of the exact words used.

An [[Intent Classification|intent classifier]] selects among the intents defined in an [[Intent Schema]]. Associated [[Entity|entities]] supply the arguments needed to carry out the goal.

9936.title: Intent Triggering
9936.heading: Intent Triggering
9936.content:
Intent triggering chooses which domain, skill, or high-level intent should receive an open-ended user request. It is essential for a broad [[Personal Virtual Assistant]] whose many capabilities cannot share one small grammar.

The trigger can rank candidate [[Assistant Skill|skills]] using the utterance together with context. After selection, a domain-specific [[Intent Classification|classifier]] extracts the detailed action and arguments.

9939.title: Intent Schema
9939.heading: Intent Schema
9939.content:
An intent schema defines the actions and argument structures an assistant supports within a domain. It specifies allowable intents, the entities or slots associated with them, and sometimes their constraints.

The schema supplies the target vocabulary for [[Intent Classification]] and [[Named Entity Recognition]]. A narrow [[Assistant Skill]] can use a detailed schema that would be difficult to maintain across every possible domain.

9941.sourceSearchName: intent response matrix intent response matrix
9941.title: Intent Response Matrix
9941.heading: Document

9942.sourceSearchName: intent response matrix intent response matrix
9942.title: Intent Response Matrix
9942.heading: Intent Response Matrix
9942.content:
An intent-response matrix maps each recognized conversational intent to one or more possible replies. It separates the language model's classification from the text the bot returns, so response content can change without retraining the recognizer.

The project stores arrays of replies in an embedded JSON resource, retrieves the array for the winning intent, and selects one entry at random. A fallback intent supplies responses when no more specific class is recognized.

9945.title: Intel Xeon Phi
9945.heading: Intel Xeon Phi
9945.content:
Intel Xeon Phi is a many-core coprocessor architecture designed for highly parallel numerical workloads. Many x86-compatible cores and wide vector units let suitable programs accelerate computation while using familiar programming models.

Neural-network training must provide enough parallel work and locality to offset data movement, thread management, and synchronization on the device.

9948.title: Intent Classification
9948.heading: Intent Classification
9948.content:
Intent classification assigns an utterance to one of the actions defined by an [[Intent Schema]]. A statistical classifier learns from example phrases labeled with their intended action.

The task is separate from [[Named Entity Recognition]], which identifies argument values. Broad assistants may first use [[Intent Triggering]] to choose a domain and then apply a more specialized classifier inside it.

9951.title: Intelligent Triage
9951.heading: Intelligent Triage
9951.content:
Intelligent triage uses data and predictive models to help prioritize or route patients through care processes. Operational predictions can reduce avoidable waiting and overcrowding by anticipating task duration and queue conditions.

The model supports rather than replaces clinical triage. Medical urgency, safety, accessibility, and exceptional circumstances can outweigh the route with the shortest predicted time.

9954.title: Intelligence Explosion
9954.heading: Intelligence Explosion
9954.content:
An intelligence explosion is the proposed feedback process in which an intelligent system improves its own capabilities, then uses the improved capabilities to make still better improvements. Repeated self-improvement could produce a rapid transition from human-level intelligence to [[Superintelligence]].

This idea supplies the mechanism in many accounts of a [[Technological Singularity]]. It depends on strong assumptions: that general intelligence can be built, that the system can redesign relevant parts of itself, and that improvements will continue rather than meet physical, computational, or organizational limits. These assumptions make the scenario important to analyze without treating it as an established forecast.

The source evaluates parallel backpropagation on this platform across core counts and voltage-frequency configurations, emphasizing that fastest execution and lowest energy can occur at different settings.

9960.title: Intel Founding
9960.heading: Intel Founding
9960.content:
Robert Noyce and Gordon Moore founded Intel in 1968 after leaving Fairchild Semiconductor, later joined by Andrew Grove. The company initially focused on semiconductor memory rather than processors.

Intel’s position within Silicon Valley’s spin-off network combined manufacturing knowledge with a strategy for high-volume standardized chips. That foundation supported its later microprocessor business.

9963.title: Intel 4004
9963.heading: Intel 4004
9963.content:
Intel introduced the 4004 in 1971 as a microprogrammable computer on a chip. Designed initially for a calculator system, it placed the central processing functions of a small general-purpose computer into one integrated circuit.

Memory and input-output chips allowed customers to build complete systems around it. The 4004 and its successors established the microprocessor as a reusable foundation rather than a single fixed-purpose circuit.

Intel’s 1103 was a semiconductor memory chip introduced in 1970 that stored roughly one thousand bits. Its density, electrical compatibility, and mass production made it competitive with hand-assembled magnetic core memory.

The chip’s success established memory as a high-volume integrated-circuit market. Regular repeated cells avoided the narrow demand faced by highly specialized logic designs.

9969.title: Integration Team
9969.heading: Integration Team
9969.content:
An integration team maintains the ability to assemble and verify a whole game from the work of many teams. It can coordinate builds, shared environments, cross-feature testing, and visibility of integration health.

It should enable frequent integration rather than become the only group responsible for making incompatible work fit at the end. Every contributing team retains responsibility for integratable output.

9972.title: Integration Test
9972.heading: Integration Test
9972.content:
An integration test verifies behavior across a real boundary between cooperating components. In an ASP.NET Core application, it can start the web application in a test host and make HTTP requests through routing, model binding, controllers, and configured services.

The broader path provides confidence that individually correct pieces work together. It is slower and requires more setup than a focused unit test, so the two scopes answer different questions.

9975.sourceSearchName: integrating 3 d with tracked video integrating 3 d with tracked video
9975.title: Integrating 3D with Tracked Video
9975.heading: Integrating 3D with Tracked Video
9975.content:
A tracked and oriented camera gives a Blender scene the perspective and movement of the recorded shot. Three-dimensional objects can then be placed against measured reference geometry so their position and scale match the footage.

Convincing integration also depends on recreating the shot's lighting and combining render and footage in the Compositor. Camera background images are visible only through the camera and provide the immediate visual reference during placement.

Gress's plate-matching examples make the next checks explicit: compare key and fill direction, adjust RGB black/white/gamma levels, and reproduce atmospheric contrast and moving grain at the element's depth. A camera match alone does not prevent a pasted-on appearance. See [[Plate Lighting Reference for CG]] and [[Matching Moving Film Grain]].

9978.title: Integrated Circuit
9978.heading: Integrated Circuit
9978.content:
An integrated circuit fabricates transistors, passive components, and their interconnections together on one piece of semiconductor material. Treating the circuit as a single manufactured object replaces assembly from many discrete parts.

Integration improves size, power, reliability, and cost at scale. It also allows complex functions to grow from repeated layers of simple logic.

9981.heading: Integrated Customer View
9981.content:
An integrated customer view assembles compatible information about a person or account from otherwise separate applications. Sales, payments, call-center contacts, credit information, and external records may each contribute only one part of the picture.

Joining these sources requires matching identities and reconciling field meanings before modeling. A unified view can support better analysis, but it also increases privacy risk because combining ordinary records may reveal more about a person than any individual source disclosed.

9984.title: Integrated Circuit Yield
9984.heading: Integrated Circuit Yield
9984.content:
Integrated-circuit yield is the proportion of fabricated chips on a wafer that pass testing. Dust, material defects, or process variation can disable individual circuits, making yield a major determinant of cost.

Manufacturers improve yield through clean environments, process control, testing, and design choices. A brilliant circuit is commercially weak if too few working copies emerge from production.
